newsitem.title: SPAIN: Kidnapped Spanish politican shot by ETA rebels.
newsitem.headline: Kidnapped Spanish politican shot by ETA rebels.

text.p: A Spanish politician kidnapped by Basque separatists was found shot in the head, barely clinging to life, on Saturday in an ETA guerrilla action that provoked national outrage.

Hospital officials said Miguel Angel Blanco, a 29-year-old Basque town councillor, was in "extremely serious" condition in a coma with two bullets lodged in his brain. Surgeons decided not to try to remove the bullets.

The shooting came despite a rally of half a million Spaniards led by Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar in the Basque capital Bilbao to protest at the abduction. Officals said it was the biggest protest against ETA separatist rebels in history.

Basque ETA rebels kidnapped Blanco on Thursday and threatened to kill him at 4 p.m. (1400 GMT) on Saturday if the government did not change its policy on rebel prisoners. The goverment called it blackmail and rejected the demands.
Blanco was found, with his hands tied, by a hunter who heard a shot in a wooded area near the northern Basque coastal city of San Sebastian. A man was seen running from the scene.
Police later found a car they believed was used as a getaway vehicle by the kidnappers. They thought it contained a bomb, but no explosives were found.
Organisers of Pamplona's world-famous running of the bulls suspended the festival on Saturday in a show of solidarity for Blanco. It was reported to be the first such interuption in nearly 20 years.

There was also confusion at first about whether Blanco had been killed or not. When he was rushed to hospital, a duty judge who went there reported Blanco was dead. Hospital officials later said he was alive and in a coma.
ETA kidnapped Blanco, a member of Aznar's ruling Popular Party, and said they would kill him unless the government gave in to its demand to move some 500 ETA inmates to prisons in the Basque country.
The kidnapping and death threat caused outrage across Spain, which had just been celebrating the release of two other ETA hostages last week, and sparked an angry backlash.
Even nationalist politicians in the region who support the separatist cause but oppose violence turned out for the protest and called on ETA to release Blanco.

"They (ETA) have to know we cannot live with this barbarity any longer. If they carry out this threat, the Basque people will never, never forgive them," Basque interior counsellor Juan Maria Atutxa told state television in Bilbao.

Aznar headed the protest march in Bilbao marching alongside his wife and fierce Basque nationalist leader Jose Antonio Ardanza. They carried a yellow banner at the front that said "Peace Now and Forever" in the Basque language.
After news of the attack, a visibally furious Ardanza blasted ETA and, more unusally for the nationalist leader, its political wing Herri Batasuna.

"It's time for them to be denounced publicly. Herri Batasuna (HB), you always want to be presented as victims in this society but you are the executioners," Ardanza told a news conference. "Enough already, not just ETA but also HB."
He said all Basque political parties except HB would meet on Sunday to discuss a response.
Reaction was intense across Spain with spontaneous demonstrations taking place in city and town centre squares.
In Madrid's Puerta del Sol, several thousand people joined hands and denounced ETA as cowardly assassins.
Leading politicians denounced ETA's action and urged calm.
"The government expresses its strongest condemnation against this barbarity," chief government spokesman Miguel Angel Rodriguez told reporters.

ETA has killed some 800 people since starting a drive for Basque independence in 1968. The rebels have set deadlines to execute kidnap victims twice before, in 1981 and 1983, and in both cases the hostages were killed.
